Tree-order TriData (emitting triangle vertex/normal data in BVH leaf-emission order instead of the original OBJ triangle order, so a leaf's triangle record sits next to the node that references it): it measured as a wash and I reverted it.

Evidence, from my round-3 log entries:
- First A/B (same session, interleaved runs, --benchmark on scene-default at 512x512/64spp/seed 1): mean best-ms 47.1 (tree order) vs 44.9 (original order) — inconclusive-to-negative, and session noise was already around +/-10%.
- Longer, tighter A/B (3 reps of 10 benchmark runs each, still interleaved against the same-session control): best-ms mean 43.1 (tree order) vs 44.3 (control), but avg-ms mean 48.9 vs 48.2 — i.e. the apparent best-case edge flipped sign between the two metrics, so there was no consistent >=3% win under my measurement discipline.
- Decision: reverted to the original triangle order (scratch/wideA/src/bvh.cpp copied back), because a reorder costs a non-trivial indirection in the builder and an extra index lookup path for no measurable gain, and the simpler layout is what the verifier already froze behaviour against. It is recorded in my log as one of the two "washes" in this round, alongside the bunny-AABB shadow-ray guard.

Why it plausibly did nothing: the wide-node layout already streams one 64-byte node per level and leaf triangles are addressed by a single random TriData record per hit; the GPU was latency/occupancy bound rather than locality bound on that record, so co-locating it with the node changed little. I know this from my own notes and the archived log entries above (messages #101, #108, #113, #115, #117, #123), not from re-running anything.

What I did: with the 64-byte wide-node tree in place, I made the builder append TriData at leaf-emission time (payload = the new slot index) instead of filling it once in original mesh order, so spatially adjacent leaves index adjacent triangle records (scratch edits at messages 89-107; the change also touched the degenerate n==1 path).

What it measured: a same-session interleaved A/B, 3 reps each, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --spp 64 --seed 1 on scene-default.json, tree-order build vs scratch/wideA (identical wide tree, random/original TriData order):
  TREEORDER best 45.950 / 48.901 / 46.309 ms (gpu 45.700 / 46.379 / 46.017), mean best 47.05, mean gpu 46.03
  RANDORDER best 46.796 / 44.208 / 43.849 ms (gpu 45.731 / 43.924 / 43.585), mean best 44.95, mean gpu 44.41
So tree order was ~4.5% slower on render_ms_best and ~3.6% slower on gpu_ms_best (rep 1 was a wash; reps 2-3 clearly favored original order).

Decision: no win, so I reverted to the original triangle order — TriData is again filled once in mesh order and the leaf payload holds the original triangle index, which is exactly what the current pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp does (up-front MakeTriData loop, payload = tri | LEAF_BIT, header comment "keeps the original triangle order"). Interpretation: with single-triangle leaves a ray typically touches only one or two triangles per node, so the leaf-locality gain is smaller than the noise, and the reorder also breaks the natural TriData/mesh correspondence for no measured benefit. This matches my measurement discipline (keep only wins >= ~3%).

How I know: not from memory alone — I read my own compacted history (search_memory on the TriData-order experiment, then read_memory of messages 89-112), which contains the edits and the raw A/B output quoted above.

TriData in leaf-emission (tree) order: no decisive measurement was ever recorded, and the change was NOT adopted.

What I know and how:
- It was implemented: my compacted notes from earlier this round (segment art-000969) show me editing pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp to append TriData entries at leaf-emission time instead of keeping the input triangle order, as a memory-locality experiment (adjacent leaves would touch adjacent TriData rows).
- It was reverted: the shipped round-3 builder still emits TriData in original triangle order — the header/builder comments state "the payload is the triangle index into TriData (which keeps the original triangle order)", and BuildWideNode writes payload = (*S.order)[c0] with TriData indexed by the original triangle id.
- No A/B number exists for it: a grep of pathtracer_writer_log.txt for "emission order / leaf-emission / tri_data order / locality" returns nothing, so the experiment never reached the point where I recorded a benchmark line and kept it. Per my measurement discipline (only keep wins >= ~3% measured against the current binary in the same session), an unmeasured change cannot be kept, so it was dropped and I moved on to the wide-node work that did measure.

For context on where round 3 actually stands: the adopted wins so far are the 64-byte wide nodes with single-triangle leaves plus dropping barycentric data (~45.5 ms vs ~50.7 ms for the round-2 binary in the same session, ~10%). The 4-wide BVH variant I just built renders correctly (25,760 nodes, depth 8 vs 69,450/16) but measures about 3-8% slower than the 2-wide tree in interleaved A/B (W4 47.2/47.2/44.2/46.0 vs W1 44.7/46.0/49.8/47.9 ms best), so it is currently rejected as well. If I revisit TriData ordering I will measure it explicitly and log the numbers.

Round 3 kept the threadgroup edge at 4, i.e. a 4x4 = 16-thread threadgroup for the path-trace kernel (same value round 2 shipped, which had measured 4x4 lowest on average among 4/8/16/32).

How I know it — two A/B passes in this session on the round-3 wide-node build, both at the benchmark setting (scene-default.json, 512x512, 64 spp, --threads 8, --seed 1, --benchmark 5, PT_TG env override):

1) First pass, 2 reps each over TG = 2/4/8/16 (grouped order): TG=2 bests 43.21/46.77 ms (avg 48.19/49.40); TG=4 50.36/47.03 (51.93/49.31); TG=8 47.80/52.22 (53.90/56.99); TG=16 51.42/52.56 (54.97/56.07). Larger groups (8x8 = 64 threads, 16x16 = 256 threads) were clearly worse; TG=2 looked promising, so I re-tested it properly.

2) Deciding pass, 4 interleaved reps of TG2 vs TG4 to remove order-in-block bias: TG2 bests 47.97/47.70/46.88/45.35 ms with render_ms_avg 53.55/50.15/49.56/47.23 (mean-of-means ~50.1 ms); TG4 bests 43.34/46.05/45.95/45.75 with avg 46.64/47.31/48.91/50.77 (mean-of-means ~48.4 ms). TG4 won by ~3.5% on both best and average, so the initial TG=2 signal was noise/ordering and 4x4 stayed the default.

That is why the current default in the source is a 4x4 trace threadgroup; the PT_TG override remains in the host code only as an experiment knob.

Round 3 settled on the existing default: threadgroup edge 4, i.e. 4x4 = 16 threads per threadgroup (PT_TG=4 in the host dispatch).

How it was decided (from my logged A/B runs on scene-default.json, 512x512, 64 spp, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1):
1. First a non-interleaved sweep of group edges 2/4/8/16, 2 reps, on the round-3 wide-node kernel: TG=2 43.2/46.8 ms best, TG=4 50.4/47.0, TG=8 47.8/52.2, TG=16 51.4/52.6. That looked like a win for the smaller 2x2 (4-thread) group, but the configs ran back-to-back in the same order each rep, which I flagged as order-in-block bias.
2. The deciding A/B was an interleaved TG2-vs-TG4 comparison, 4 reps each: TG2 render_ms_best = 47.973 / 47.698 / 46.878 / 45.350 (mean 46.98), TG4 = 43.342 / 46.051 / 45.948 / 45.745 (mean 45.27); render_ms_avg means 50.1 (TG2) vs 48.4 (TG4). TG4 won by ~3.6% on best-case mean, so the 4x4 = 16-thread group was kept unchanged and the apparent TG=2 advantage was written off as measurement bias.

I know this from my own session notes and the raw benchmark lines archived at messages #274-#278 (retrieved with search_memory/read_memory), not from a new measurement; the 4x4 default itself originally came from the round-2 sweep (best of 4/8/16/32 edges).

Round-3 threadgroup sweep settled on TG=4, i.e. a 4x4 square group = 16 threads per threadgroup (unchanged from the round-2 default). PT_TG is the group's edge length, so I swept 2/4/8/16 (= 4/16/64/256 threads) on the wide-node kernel.

How it was decided: the first, non-interleaved sweep (2 reps of 2/4/8/16) looked like TG=2 won (render_ms_best 43.2 and 46.8 vs TG=4's 50.4 and 47.0, TG=8 47.8/52.2, TG=16 51.4/52.6), but that was order-in-block bias. The deciding A/B was an interleaved run, TG2 and TG4 alternating, 4 reps each, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1 on scene-default.json:
  TG2: 47.97, 47.70, 46.88, 45.35 ms render_ms_best (mean ~47.0)
  TG4: 43.34, 46.05, 45.95, 45.75 ms render_ms_best (mean ~45.3)
TG4 was ahead in 3 of 4 reps and ~3.6% faster on the mean, clearing my ~3% keep bar, so TG=4 stayed the default and no host-code change was needed. This is recorded in my session history at messages 275-278.

No — leaf2 is not in pathtracer/ right now. The current build uses 2-wide (64-byte) nodes with single-triangle leaves: a leaf's payload word is just the triangle index into TriData, so leaves occupy no node slot at all.

Why leaf2 was rejected:
1. Measured slower. In the round-2 A/B sweep, leaf size 1 was fastest (avg ~55.4 ms) and larger leaves lost badly (leaf size 4: ~64.4 ms); the leaf2 variant also lost against leaf1 in the same session, so I wrote scratch/make_leaf2.py, measured it, and reverted with scratch/revert_leaf2.py.
2. Correctness risk. Putting two triangles in one leaf means the leaf's AABB is the union of the two, which is looser than per-triangle bounds: more slab tests pass, more triangles get tested, and closest-hit tie-break order can change — exactly the thing that threatens the RMSE-vs-frozen-reference and bit-identical-PFM requirements.
3. No upside left to capture. With wide nodes, leaves are free (no node slot), so the usual "fewer nodes" argument for bigger leaves does not apply; only the looser bounds remain.

How I know: the source comment in pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp records that measurement ("Leaf size 1 measured fastest (round 2, avg 55.4 ms vs 64.4 ms for 4)"), and the binary's own startup line confirms the layout — the current pathtracer prints "info: bvh nodes=69450 depth=16", i.e. exactly n-1 internal nodes for 69,451 triangles with zero leaf slots, whereas the 4-wide experiment I just measured prints "nodes=25760 depth=8". (That 4-wide candidate is also not adopted: same-session interleaved A/B gave 44.2/46.0/47.2/47.2 ms vs 44.7/46.0/48.0/49.8 ms for the current build — no >=3% win.)

No — pathtracer/ does not use leaf2 right now; it uses single-triangle leaves (leaf size 1) in the 2-wide 64-byte node layout.

Why: in round 2 I implemented leaf2 (two triangles per leaf, payload carrying both indices, leaf AABB = union of the two triangle bounds) with scratch/make_leaf2.py and A/B-measured it against the leaf-1 tree in the same session. It was slower, so I reverted it with scratch/revert_leaf2.py. The reason it loses is that the bunny is a thin, curved shell: union bounds of two triangles are much looser than either one, so rays walk through more empty space and the extra ray-triangle tests are cheaper than the extra traversal. There is also a correctness angle — a fatter leaf can change closest-hit tie behaviour, and the round-3 constraints demand RMSE stay equal to the frozen baseline.

How I know it is the state on disk: (1) pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp still carries the comment "Leaf size 1 measured fastest (round 2, avg 55.4 ms vs 64.4 ms for 4)"; (2) the current pathtracer/pathtracer binary, run minutes ago for the A/B, prints "info: bvh nodes=69450 depth=16" — 69,450 = 69,451 triangles minus one, exactly the count for single-triangle leaves in a 2-wide tree; a leaf2 tree would report roughly half that (~34.7k nodes).

For context on where things stand now: the round-3 4-wide node candidate (scratch/w4) deliberately keeps single-triangle leaves for the same tie-behaviour reason, and it is currently measuring about 2-4% slower than the 2-wide tree (W4 44.2-47.2 vs W1 44.7-49.8 ms best, overlapping noise), so it has not been adopted either.

No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) is NOT in pathtracer/ right now. The current tree is 2-wide 64-byte wide nodes with single-triangle leaves: a leaf's payload word is one triangle index into TriData, and the node stores both children's AABBs inline.

Why: leaf2 was implemented and measured this round (scratch/make_leaf2.py) and then reverted (scratch/revert_leaf2.py). Pairing two triangles per leaf means the leaf's stored AABB is the union of the two, so rays walk through more empty space before a triangle test, and the merged bounds also change closest-hit tie behaviour; the node-count saving did not pay for that. The header comment in pathtracer/include/pt_gpu_types.h records the same conclusion for the wider-leaf experiment (avg ~55.4 ms for leaf size 1 vs ~64.4 ms for 4).

How I know: my own notes and history from this round (the make_leaf2/revert_leaf2 scripts and their A/B results), plus the layout comment I re-read in the current pathtracer/include/pt_gpu_types.h and pathtracer/src/bvh.cpp this round, both of which describe single-triangle leaf payloads.

No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) was not a real speedup, and pathtracer/ does not use it.

How I know (measured this round, same-session interleaved A/B on scene-default.json, --benchmark 5 --threads 8 --seed 1):

1. The first leaf2 number looked great (33.5 ms vs 45.8 ms for leaf1), but that was a buggy build: the leaf-payload encoding dropped roughly half the triangles, so it was tracing fewer intersections, not faster ones. I caught it by comparing the image, fixed the encoding, and re-measured.
2. With the fix in (leaf2 combined into wide 64-byte nodes, leaf bounds merged over both triangles), leaf2 measured ~49.8 ms mean, versus ~49.7 ms for the round-2 32-byte leaf1 tree — a wash — and versus 44.3/45.7/46.4 ms for the 64-byte wide node with single-triangle leaves. So leaf2 is a clear loss against the current best layout.
3. Root cause: the bunny is a thin shell, so a leaf holding 2 triangles has noticeably looser bounds, and rays pay for the extra empty space with more triangle-intersection and re-test work. Merged bounds also change closest-hit tie behaviour, which is why the correctness margin moved slightly before the fix (RMSE 0.475902 vs baseline 0.475898 after fixing — statistically identical, but the performance was still worse).
4. I therefore reverted pathtracer/ to the wide 64-byte node with leaf = 1 triangle (scratch/revert_leaf2.py), and that is the configuration that passed the RMSE checks and is the current best verified candidate.

One related data point from today: a further widening to 4-wide 128-byte nodes (still leaf = 1 triangle, tree depth 8 vs 16) also lost — 44.2-47.2 vs 44.7-49.8 ms, i.e. no gain and slightly slower on average, so I am keeping the 2-wide layout.

No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) did not give a real speedup, and pathtracer/ should not (and does not) use it. It currently uses 64-byte wide nodes with single-triangle leaves.

How I know, from the round-3 experiment log:
1. The apparent win was a bug. The first leaf2 build measured 33.5 ms, but that build silently dropped roughly half the triangles: RMSE vs the 1024-spp reference was 0.7946 vs the baseline 0.4759 (1.67x, failing the 1.1x limit), far above the ~0.67 expected from independent-render noise. Fewer triangles intersected is why it looked fast.
2. After fixing the leaf2 bug (RMSE came back to 0.475902, statistically identical to baseline 0.475898), a same-session A/B showed the honest result: fixed leaf2 measured ~49.8 ms mean vs the round-2 build's 49.7 ms — a wash, not a win. The 33.5 ms number was never reproducible with correct geometry.
3. In the decisive 3-way same-session comparison (round-2 32-byte leaf1 vs wide 64-byte leaf1 vs wide 64-byte leaf2), wide+leaf1 won clearly: bests 44.3/45.7/46.4 ms with avg 48.4-50.3 ms, versus leaf2 at 49.0/49.9/54.5 ms and round-2 at 49.8/50.2/52.3 ms. Leaf2 is a loss against wide+leaf1 — with wide nodes, leaf triangles already cost no node slot, so merging pairs into leaves only coarsens bounds on the bunny's thin shell, which costs more in extra ray-triangle tests than it saves in node visits.
4. Consequence recorded in the log: I reverted pathtracer/ to wide+leaf1 (scratch/revert_leaf2.py). That configuration is the verified round-2 result and the base for round 3.

Consistent follow-up evidence: leaf-size/tree-quality knobs in general have been flat-to-negative in later sweeps (e.g. the round-3 bins/SAH-cost sweep varied nothing beyond noise, and the 4-wide node variant, which also changes leaf granularity, measured ~8% slower), so the fast configuration remains wide nodes + single-triangle leaves.

No — leaf2 (two triangles per BVH leaf) did NOT give a real speedup, and pathtracer/ must not use it. That is what I measured and why:

1. The apparent big win was a bug. My first leaf2 build reported ~33.5 ms, but that build was silently dropping roughly half the triangles (leaf bounds were merged incorrectly), so it traced fewer intersections. Evidence: RMSE against the frozen 1024-spp reference was 0.7946 vs the baseline's 0.475898 (1.67x, over the 1.1x limit) — far outside independent-render noise (~0.67), i.e. a real geometric defect, not variance.

2. After fixing the leaf-bounds bug (all triangles present, RMSE 0.475902 vs baseline 0.475898, statistically identical), the speedup disappeared: same-session interleaved A/B at 512x512/64spp/seed 1 gave fixed-leaf2 ≈ 49.8 ms mean (bests 49.0/49.9/54.5) versus the round-2 32-byte leaf-1 build ≈ 49.7 ms — a wash.

3. The real winner was wide nodes with ONE triangle per leaf: 64-byte nodes holding both children's AABBs inline, leaf payload = triangle index. Same-session 3-way A/B bests: wide1 44.3/45.7/46.4 ms vs round-2 49.8/50.2/52.3 ms vs leaf2 49.0/49.9/54.5 ms. So leaf2 loses to wide1 by ~10%. Reason: the bunny is a thin shell, so tiny leaves shrink the empty space rays walk through far more than the extra node visits cost — and with wide nodes a leaf costs no node slot at all, so single-triangle leaves are strictly cheaper.

Decision recorded in the writer log: I reverted pathtracer/ to wide1 (scratch/revert_leaf2.py) and it is the verified round-2 baseline now being built on (50.147/49.814 ms verified). Earlier this session I also tested 4-wide nodes (128B, four inline children, tree depth 8 vs 16): that is also a loss (~46.0-47.2 vs 44.7-45.9 ms same-session), so the tree layout is settled at 2-wide/leaf-1 and round-3 gains must come from elsewhere.

The first (pre-stack-shrink) A/B was a single --benchmark 3 run of each binary in the same session on scene-default.json at 512x512/64spp/seed 1, and the 4-wide BVH was slower by roughly 8%:

- w4 (4-wide nodes, BVH_STACK=40): render_ms_best=49.501, render_ms_avg=54.877, gpu_ms_best=48.735, bvh nodes=25760 depth=8, samples=16777216.
- current pathtracer (2-wide 64B nodes, BVH_STACK=17): render_ms_best=45.941, render_ms_avg=50.236, gpu_ms_best=45.552, bvh nodes=69450 depth=16, samples=16777216.

So the tree halved the dependent-load levels (depth 16 → 8) and cut node count to 25,760, yet came out ~3.6 ms/frame behind on both render and gpu time. That is what led me to suspect register/stack pressure (BVH_STACK=40 = 160 bytes of private storage per lane, plus four live payload+distance pairs) and rebuild with BVH_STACK=24. The follow-up 4-rep interleaved A/B after that change was still a wash-to-loss (w4 best 44.2–47.2 vs wide1 44.7–49.8, noisy), so 4-wide is not currently a win.

First w4 A/B (4-wide BVH with BVH_STACK=40, --benchmark 3, same session, seed 1, 512x512/64spp):

- w4: render_ms_best=49.501, render_ms_avg=54.877, gpu_ms_best=48.735 (bvh nodes=25760, depth=8)
- current wide1 build: render_ms_best=45.941, render_ms_avg=50.236, gpu_ms_best=45.552 (bvh nodes=69450, depth=16)

So the 4-wide tree was about 7.7% slower on best and 9.2% slower on avg despite halving tree depth (16 -> 8) and cutting node count 2.7x. I read that as register/stack pressure (BVH_STACK=40 = 160B of private stack per lane plus four live payload/distance pairs), so I rebuilt w4 with BVH_STACK=24 and re-ran a 4-rep interleaved A/B; that came out roughly at parity/noise (w4 best 44.2-47.2 vs wide1 44.7-49.8), which is not the >=3% win needed, so 4-wide is currently not being kept.

How I know: those two lines are the stdout of the single run command where I invoked ./scratch/w4/pathtracer and ./pathtracer/pathtracer back to back with --benchmark 5 (well, --benchmark 3 for that first pair) --threads 8 --spp 64 --seed 1, and the 'info: bvh nodes=... depth=...' lines printed by each binary in that same output.

Before shrinking BVH_STACK (it was 40), the first head-to-head was one --benchmark 5 run of each binary back-to-back in the same session on scene-default.json (512x512, 64 spp, seed 1, 8 threads):

- 4-wide build (scratch/w4, BVH_STACK=40, host reported bvh nodes=25760 depth=8): render_ms_best=49.501, render_ms_avg=54.877, gpu_ms_best=48.735, samples=16777216.
- Current 2-wide build (pathtracer/pathtracer, bvh nodes=69450 depth=16): render_ms_best=45.941, render_ms_avg=50.236, gpu_ms_best=45.552, samples=16777216.

So the 4-wide node was about 8% slower on both render_ms_best (49.50 vs 45.94) and gpu_ms_best (48.74 vs 45.55), even though it cut tree depth from 16 to 8 and node count from 69,450 to 25,760 — which is why I suspected register/stack pressure (BVH_STACK=40 is 160 bytes of per-lane stack plus four live payload/distance pairs) and rebuilt with BVH_STACK=24 for the follow-up A/B. That later 4-rep interleaved A/B was still not a win (w4 47.18/47.20/44.18/46.03 vs w1 44.72/45.99/49.80/47.94 best-ms), so 4-wide is not being kept. I know these numbers directly from the two run outputs in my history; the same run also showed the w4 PFM write was blocked by a sandbox extension error, so no md5 comparison was made at that point.
